Agentic CFD report · 2026-11-11

Steady 3D flow past a cylinder in a square channel at Re = 20 (DFG benchmark 3D-1Z)

Summary1 Problem2 Assumptions 3 Theory4 Decisions5 Pre-flight test 6 Simulation7 Comparison8 Workflow insights A ReproducibilityB Performance

Summary ✗ FAIL Benchmark

Benchmark comparison FAILED. On the finest mesh (L4, 2,433,024 cells) the drag is \(6.1805\) (reference \(6.1853\), \(-0.077\,\%\)) and the lift \(0.00956\) (\(0.00940\), \(1.7\,\%\)); mesh-extrapolated: \(0.017\,\%\) and \(1.2\,\%\). The drag passes the band fixed beforehand (\(0.60\) times its width). The lift misses the band fixed beforehand (\(2.51\) times its width). The lift is very sensitive to the cell distribution around the cylinder (sensitivity runs); the paper's OpenFOAM was \(3.5\,\%\) off on its finest level.

Key findings

  • Drag (a). \(c_D = 6.1805\) on L4 (2,433,024 cells), \(-0.077\,\%\) from the reference \(6.1853\); Richardson extrapolation of L2-L4 gives \(6.1864\) (\(0.017\,\%\)). The paper's OpenFOAM result on its level 4 (3,145,728 cells) is \(6.1893\) (\(0.064\,\%\)).
  • Lift (b). \(c_L = 0.00956\), \(1.7\,\%\) from the reference \(0.00940\); extrapolated \(0.00951\) (\(1.2\,\%\)). The paper's OpenFOAM level 4 is \(3.5\,\%\) off. The lift is a small difference of pressure and friction forces (\(0.00728\) and \(0.00228\)) and converges from far above: \(0.0201\), \(0.0116\), \(0.0098\), \(0.0096\) on L1-L4.
  • Mesh convergence. \(c_D\): observed order \(2.10\), \(c_L\): observed order \(2.73\) on L2-L4 (design order 2); GCI of L4 \(0.12\,\%\) (drag) and \(0.61\,\%\) (lift).
  • Flow (c). Behind the cylinder the fluid turns back over \(0.75\,D\) (mid-plane, Figure 2); the fastest backflow is \(0.019\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(9.4\,\%\) of the mean inflow.
  • Converged and conserving. Over the last \(10\,\%\) of the iterations \(c_D\) changed by at most \(2.6 \times 10^{-8}\) and \(c_L\) by \(1.7 \times 10^{-8}\); the momentum balance of the channel closes to \(0.14\,\%\) of the drag on L4 (\(0.036\,\%\) with the inlet friction it neglects); the side force is \(1.3 \times 10^{-11}\) of the drag (mid-plane symmetry).
  • GPU question. The GPU is faster per iteration from about \(2.0\) million cells: on the largest mesh (4,752,000 cells) one iteration takes \(3.80\,\mathrm{s}\) on the best CPU setup (GAMG DIC-GS, 8 ranks) and \(3.37\,\mathrm{s}\) with the pressure solved on the GPU (8 ranks), a factor \(1.13\); the pressure solve alone takes \(1.44\) against \(0.87\,\mathrm{s}\) (factor \(1.65\)). Both give the same converged forces. Details: GPU study report.
  • Rule failed: \(c_L\) differs from the reference by more than twice the combined uncertainty.
LimitationThe reference is itself a numerical solution (adaptive finite elements), not an experiment; its uncertainty is estimated from a second code (FeatFlow level 4).
LimitationFour meshes up to 2,433,024 cells; a fifth level (about 19 million cells) would need about 11 GB of memory and hours per run on this machine.
LimitationThe flow picture (c) has no reference to compare with; the length of the reversed-flow region is reported for information only.
LimitationSteady laminar model as the benchmark; whether this steady state is stable (would be reached by a real flow) is not tested by a steady solver.
LimitationWall times of the accuracy runs are inflated (they shared the machine with GPU tuning runs); speed numbers are in the GPU study.

1 Problem

Fluid flows slowly through a channel of square cross-section past a circular cylinder that spans the channel from wall to wall. At this Reynolds number the flow is steady. Find the steady flow and the forces on the cylinder, and compare them with the published benchmark. This case is also the test problem for a CPU versus GPU performance study (see study below).

What we want to find

  1. aDrag coefficient \(c_D\) of the cylinder
  2. bLift coefficient \(c_L\) of the cylinder
  3. cA picture of the flow in the mid-plane \(z = H/2\) (velocity), showing the region of reversed flow behind the cylinder

Setup

  • Channel: length \(L\) along \(x\), square cross-section of side \(H\) in \(y\) and \(z\). Coordinates start at a lower corner of the inlet plane.
  • Cylinder: diameter \(D\), axis along \(z\) through \((x_c, y_c)\), spanning the whole channel width \(0 \le z \le H\). It sits slightly below the mid-height of the channel.
  • Inlet (\(x = 0\)): \(u = 16 U_m\, y z (H - y)(H - z) / H^4\), \(v = w = 0\).
  • Outlet (\(x = L\)): free outflow, no stress imposed.
  • Channel walls and cylinder: no-slip.
  • Force coefficients use the mean inflow velocity \(\bar U\) (the average of the inlet profile over the inlet plane), the diameter and the cylinder length \(H\): \(c_D = 2 F_D / (\rho \bar U^2 D H)\) and \(c_L = 2 F_L / (\rho \bar U^2 D H)\), with the drag \(F_D\) along \(x\) and the lift \(F_L\) along \(y\).
  • The Reynolds number is \(Re = \bar U D / \nu\).

3 Theory

Flow around a cylinder in a duct has no exact solution: the convection term makes the equations nonlinear and the geometry is three-dimensional. The comparison therefore uses the benchmark's reference values. Theory still fixes the scales (one number, \(Re\)), the inflow (its mean and how far it is from developed duct flow), what must hold by symmetry (no side force), and a conservation law used as a check (the momentum balance of the channel). The algebra marked below is checked by SymPy.

Governing equations: steady, incompressible, Newtonian, constant density
\[ \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0,\qquad (\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\,\mathbf{u} = -\frac{1}{\rho}\nabla p + \nu\,\nabla^2\mathbf{u} \]
The convection term on the left makes the equations nonlinear; with a cylinder in a duct no exact solution is known. The flow is computed; theory gives scales, symmetry and a balance used as checks.
Boundary conditions
\[ x = 0:\ u = \frac{16\,U_m\,y z (H - y)(H - z)}{H^4},\ v = w = 0;\qquad x = L:\ \nu\frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial n} - \frac{p}{\rho}\,\mathbf{n} = 0;\qquad \text{walls, cylinder: } \mathbf{u} = 0 \]
The outflow condition is the stress-free ('do-nothing') condition of the benchmark. The finite-volume model uses zero normal gradient of velocity and zero pressure at the outlet, the same condition for flow leaving parallel to the axis, which holds 20 diameters behind the cylinder.
Requested quantities (3D normalisation with the cylinder length)
\[ c_D = \frac{2F_D}{\rho\,\bar U^2 D H},\qquad c_L = \frac{2F_L}{\rho\,\bar U^2 D H},\qquad \mathbf{F} = \oint_{\mathrm{cyl}} \left(-p\,\mathbf{n} + \rho\nu\,(\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^T)\cdot\mathbf{n}\right)dA \]
The force is the pressure plus the friction integrated over the whole cylinder surface; drag is its x component, lift its y component.
Symmetry about the mid-plane z = H/2
\[ \mathbf{u}(x, y, H - z) = \big(u, v, -w\big)(x, y, z)\ \Rightarrow\ w = 0 \text{ on } z = H/2,\qquad F_z = 0 \]
Geometry and inflow are mirror-symmetric about the mid-plane, so (for the steady, stable solution) the flow is too: no fluid crosses the mid-plane and the side force vanishes. The simulation does not impose this; it is checked.
Steady x-momentum balance of the whole channel (check of the force output)
\[ F_D + F_w = \int_{\mathrm{in}}\!\left(p + \rho u^2\right)dA - \int_{\mathrm{out}}\!\left(p + \rho u^2\right)dA \]
In steady flow the drag on the cylinder plus the friction on the four channel walls must equal the net pressure and momentum flux through inlet and outlet (viscous normal stresses at inlet and outlet are neglected: they vanish for flow parallel to the axis). It tests the force output independently of the force integration on the cylinder.
  • inflow \(u = 0\) on all four walls (no slip)
  • inflow maximum at the centre \(y = z = H/2\) with \(u = U_m\)
  • mean inflow velocity \(\bar U = \frac{1}{H^2}\iint u\,dy\,dz = \frac{4}{9}U_m\)
  • the inflow is not the developed square-duct flow: \(\nabla^2 u\) varies over the section
  • inflow symmetric about the mid-plane: \(u(y, H - z) = u(y, z)\)

Physics

Physical model
D1
Steady, incompressible, laminar, Newtonian flow in three dimensions
Physics
Why this choice
The benchmark 3D-1Z is defined for the steady 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with constant viscosity \(\nu = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}\) at \(Re = 20\), where the flow is laminar and steady. Density is constant (\(\rho = 1\)), so OpenFOAM's kinematic pressure \(p/\rho\) equals the pressure. The time derivative is dropped (steadyState).
Effect on the result
Defines the equations solved. A turbulence model would add an eddy viscosity the benchmark does not have.
Alternatives
A transient solver run until the flow stops changing (the benchmark paper ran OpenFOAM's icoFoam that way): same steady answer, many more pressure solves.
OpenFOAM settingsconstant/turbulenceProperties/simulationTypeconstant/transportProperties/*system/fvSchemes/ddtSchemes/*
Solver
D2
simpleFoam: the steady SIMPLE algorithm in its SIMPLEC form (consistent yes)
Solver
Why this choice
The answer is a steady state, so a steady solver iterates directly towards it; each iteration solves the momentum equations once and the pressure equation once. SIMPLEC allows weak velocity relaxation and no pressure relaxation. deltaT 1 only counts iterations. It also gives the GPU study a clean unit of work: one pressure solve per iteration.
Effect on the result
How the steady state is reached, not the state itself (the converged equations are the same).
Alternatives
pimpleFoam/icoFoam run to steady state (as the benchmark paper; slower); plain SIMPLE (needs pressure relaxation, more iterations).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/controlDict/applicationsystem/controlDict/deltaTsystem/fvSolution/SIMPLE/consistent
Domain and boundary conditions
D3
Square channel \(2.5 \times 0.41 \times 0.41\,\mathrm{m}\) with the cylinder \(D = 0.1\,\mathrm{m}\), axis along \(z\) through \((0.5, 0.2)\,\mathrm{m}\), spanning the channel; patches inlet, outlet, walls (all four channel walls) and cylinder
Physics
Why this choice
The geometry is given. The cylinder surface is represented by straight faces between points on the exact circle (blockMesh arcs).
Effect on the result
Defines the problem. The faceted circle is a geometric error that shrinks with the square of the surface cell size and is part of the mesh study.
Alternatives
A curved-boundary (higher-order) representation, as finite-element codes such as FeatFlow use; not available in standard finite-volume OpenFOAM.
OpenFOAM settingssystem/blockMeshDict/verticessystem/blockMeshDict/scalesystem/blockMeshDict/boundary
D4
Inlet: \(u = 16U_m\,yz(H - y)(H - z)/H^4\), \(v = w = 0\), evaluated at each inlet face centre (exprFixedValue), zero normal pressure gradient. Outlet: zero normal velocity gradient, \(p = 0\). Walls and cylinder: no slip, zero normal pressure gradient.
Physics
Why this choice
The inflow and no-slip conditions are given. The benchmark's stress-free ("do-nothing") outflow is modelled by the standard OpenFOAM pair zero-gradient velocity / fixed zero pressure; both are the same for flow leaving parallel to the axis, 20 diameters behind the cylinder. Face-centre values of the profile give a slightly too large inflow (a second-order error, measured in the pre-flight and shrinking 4 times per level), which the mesh study includes.
Effect on the result
Defines the problem. The outflow model can differ from the benchmark's only near the outlet.
Alternatives
Exact face-averaged inflow values written as a list (removes the small inflow excess); inletOutlet at the outlet (prevents backflow; none occurs).
OpenFOAM settings0/U/boundaryField/*0/p/boundaryField/*
D5
Initial field: fluid at rest on L1; every finer level starts from the converged flow of the next coarser level, interpolated with mapFields. The fixed-length GPU/CPU timing runs all start from rest.
Solver
Why this choice
A steady solution does not depend on the starting guess, but a good guess saves many iterations on the expensive meshes. The timing runs start from the same field on CPU and GPU so that both do exactly the same work.
Effect on the result
The number of iterations, not the converged answer (checked: the stopping rule is applied to every run).
Alternatives
Start every level from rest (more iterations on L4); potential-flow initialisation (potentialFoam).
OpenFOAM settings0/U/internalField0/p/internalFieldsystem/controlDict/startTime
Mesh
D6
Block-structured O-grid (as case 4): 4 blocks around the cylinder inside a square box of side \(0.2\,\mathrm{m}\) centred on the axis (radial cells shrinking 4 times towards the cylinder), 8 rectangular blocks filling the channel (graded towards the box), all extruded over \(0 \le z \le H\) with cells shrinking 2 times towards both side walls. Four levels L1-L4 with 24 to 192 faces around the cylinder and 12 to 96 cells across the channel (4752 to 2.43 million cells); every cell count doubles per level in all three directions (refinement ratio 2, 8 times the cells), like the benchmark's levels 1-4. Three extra meshes (G16, G36, G60) for the GPU study only.
Accuracy
Why this choice
A body-fitted O-grid gives orthogonal, smoothly graded cells on the cylinder, where the forces are decided; the side-wall grading resolves the boundary layers on the walls that the cylinder ends touch. Refinement ratio 2 in every direction gives the observed order and the GCI. The level sizes match the benchmark's (6144 to 3.1 million cells), so the comparison with its OpenFOAM results is level by level.
Effect on the result
Spatial discretisation error, measured by the mesh study (observed order, Richardson extrapolation, GCI). Sensitivity runs with the O-grid radial ratio changed to 2 and 8 (L3, and ratio 2 also on L4) show that the lift depends strongly on this choice (Comparison).
Alternatives
snappyHexMesh around an STL cylinder (less regular cells at the wall); uniform cells in \(z\) (more cells for the same wall resolution); a different radial cell distribution in the O-grid (tested, see above).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/blockMeshDict/blocks
Discretisation
D7
Second-order central schemes in space: bounded Gauss linear for convection, Gauss linear gradients and interpolation, Laplacian with explicit non-orthogonal correction (corrected)
Accuracy
Why this choice
At \(Re = 20\) the flow is smooth and dominated by friction (cell Péclet numbers near the cylinder are small), so central convection is stable and adds no numerical diffusion; it is also what the benchmark paper's OpenFOAM runs used. bounded removes the continuity-error term while the iterations converge; it vanishes at convergence. The O-grid corners are up to about 42 degrees non-orthogonal, so the Laplacian needs the correction.
Effect on the result
Spatial order of accuracy (2) and the size of the error constant.
Alternatives
linearUpwind (also second order, more dissipative, more robust on coarse meshes).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/fvSchemes/gradSchemes/*system/fvSchemes/laplacianSchemes/*system/fvSchemes/interpolationSchemes/*system/fvSchemes/snGradSchemes/*system/fvSchemes/divSchemes/*
Algorithm and linear solvers
D8
SIMPLEC with velocity relaxation 0.9 and no pressure relaxation, no non-orthogonal corrector loop. Pressure: GAMG (Gauss-Seidel smoother) to \(relTol\ 0.05\) per iteration (absolute tolerance \(10^{-12}\), never reached); velocity: symmetric Gauss-Seidel to \(relTol\ 0.1\). In the GPU study the pressure solver is replaced by OGL's Ginkgo CG with a multigrid preconditioner on the GPU at the same tolerances.
Solver
Why this choice
In a steady iteration each linear system only needs to be solved partly: the outer iterations remove the rest, and the converged answer does not depend on how far each solve went. GAMG is the fastest CPU pressure solver measured on this machine (case 4: 4 times faster than PCG). The non-orthogonal correction is explicit and converges with the outer iterations, so an inner corrector loop would only add pressure solves.
Effect on the result
Speed and the path to the steady state; not the converged answer (the stopping rule bounds the remaining iteration error).
Alternatives
Tighter linear solves (fewer outer iterations, each more expensive); PCG for pressure (slower); one non-orthogonal corrector (one more pressure solve per iteration).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/fvSolution/solvers/*system/fvSolution/relaxationFactors/*system/fvSolution/SIMPLE/nNonOrthogonalCorrectors
Convergence
D9
Stop when the normalised initial residuals fall below \(10^{-7}\) (pressure) and \(10^{-8}\) (each velocity component), at most 6000 iterations; accepted only if, over the last 10 % of the iterations, \(c_D\) changed by less than \(10^{-5}\) and \(c_L\) by less than \(10^{-6}\) (physical check, fixed before the runs)
Accuracy
Why this choice
Residuals are not a solution-error measure (pitfall 10 of the primer), so the requested numbers themselves must have stopped changing, by far less than the mesh error (about \(10^{-3}\) relative between levels). The thresholds are about \(2 \times 10^{-6}\) of \(c_D\) and \(10^{-4}\) of \(c_L\).
Effect on the result
The iteration error of the answers, bounded by the physical check on every run.
Alternatives
A runTimeControl function object on the force coefficients (stops directly on the physical check; needs a test of which results it can watch); a fixed iteration count.
OpenFOAM settingssystem/fvSolution/SIMPLE/residualControl/*system/controlDict/endTime
Outputs
D10
Forces on the cylinder (drag, lift and side force) and on the channel walls, momentum flux, pressure force and volume flow at inlet and outlet, every iteration; fields written at the end of a run, 12 significant digits; built-in profiling (time per code section)
Output
Why this choice
Drag and lift every iteration give the answers (a), (b) and the convergence check; the side force tests the mid-plane symmetry; fluxes and wall friction close the momentum balance (physical check of the force output). The final fields give the mid-plane picture (c). Profiling splits the run time into pressure solve, momentum solve and the rest for the GPU study, identically on CPU and GPU.
Effect on the result
What is measured and how precisely; not the solution.
Alternatives
The forceCoeffs function object (same numbers, but the 3D normalisation would be hidden in its settings; here the coefficients are computed in the analysis from the raw forces).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/controlDict/writeControlsystem/controlDict/writeIntervalsystem/controlDict/writePrecisionsystem/controlDict/timePrecisionsystem/controlDict/functions/*system/controlDict/profiling/*
GPU pressure solver (study only)
D11
For the GPU study only: libs ("libOGL.so") loads the OGL plugin, and the pressure solver becomes Ginkgo CG on the GPU (executor cuda) with a multigrid preconditioner, scaling -1, forceHostBuffer true, all MPI ranks gathered on the one GPU (ranksPerGPU); the tuned preconditioner settings are in the GPU study report
Solver
Why this choice
OGL replaces only the linear solver of one field; assembly, momentum and everything else stay on the CPU. Its pressure solves reach the same normalised tolerance as GAMG, so the converged steady state is the same (checked in the study).
Effect on the result
Run time only, provided the same-answer check passes.
Alternatives
Other OGL preconditioners (block Jacobi, ISAI, IC) or solvers (BiCGStab); a GPU-native CFD code (not OpenFOAM).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/controlDict/libs
Parallel runs
D12
L1 on one core, L2 on 4 MPI ranks, L3 on 8 and L4 on 12 ranks (mpirun --use-hwthread-cpus above 8), scotch decomposition; the remaining hardware threads ran the GPU tuning runs at the same time
Solver
Why this choice
The accuracy runs only need to finish within the budget; leaving 4 of the 16 hardware threads free let the GPU tuning run alongside. Their wall times are therefore not used for any speed comparison (the GPU study measures speed with nothing else running). Decomposition changes the order of floating-point operations and the GAMG coarsening only; the converged answer is the same to the stopping tolerance.
Effect on the result
Run time only.
Alternatives
All 16 ranks with nothing else running (case 4's fastest setting; about a third faster for L4); everything serial (L4 would take hours).
OpenFOAM settings

6 Simulation

6.1From the real problem to the simulation model

AspectReal problemSimulation model
GeometrySquare channel \(2.5 \times 0.41 \times 0.41\,\mathrm{m}\), cylinder \(D = 0.1\,\mathrm{m}\) from wall to wallThe same, meshed in full (no symmetry plane); the circle as straight faces between points on it.
InflowProduct of two parabolas, maximum \(U_m = 0.45\,\mathrm{m/s}\)The profile evaluated at each inlet face centre; flow rate within \(1.2 \times 10^{-4}\) (relative) of \(\bar U H^2\) on L4.
OutflowFree (stress-free) outflowZero normal velocity gradient, zero pressure.
Steady stateThe flow after all transients have died outSteady SIMPLEC iterations until the residuals and the forces stop changing (physical check).
ForcesPressure and friction on the cylinderOpenFOAM forces on the cylinder patch every iteration; coefficients with \(\tfrac12\rho\bar U^2 D H\) computed in the analysis.

7 Comparison

Benchmark: the simulation is compared with the reference values of Braack and Richter (adaptive finite elements). Agreement is judged against a band: the GCI of the finest mesh plus the reference uncertainty (distance to FeatFlow level 4). The benchmark paper's own OpenFOAM results are shown for comparison.

How the differences are measured

Force coefficients
\[ c_D = \frac{2F_D}{\rho\,\bar U^2 D H},\qquad c_L = \frac{2F_L}{\rho\,\bar U^2 D H} \]
\(\bar U = \tfrac49 U_m\), \(H\) the cylinder length; forces are the converged values.
Reference uncertainty
\[ U_{\mathrm{ref}} = |q_{\mathrm{ref}} - q_{\mathrm{FeatFlow},4}| \]
Distance to an independent high-order solution on its finest level.
Simulation uncertainty
\[ U_{\mathrm{sim}} = 1.25\,\frac{|q_{L4} - q_{L3}|}{2^p - 1} \]
GCI of the finest mesh (Celik et al. 2008) from L2, L3, L4 with their observed order \(p\).
Verdict per number
\[ |q_{L4} - q_{\mathrm{ref}}| \le U_{\mathrm{sim}} + U_{\mathrm{ref}} \]
Inside the band: ok; up to twice the band: warning; beyond: fail.
NumberReference\(U_{\mathrm{ref}}\)Simulation (L4)\(U_{\mathrm{sim}}\)Difference÷ band, statusRichardson (rel. diff.)Paper OpenFOAM L4 (rel. diff.)
\(c_D\)\(6.1853\)\(6.8 \times 10^{-4}\)\(6.1805\)\(0.0073\)\(-0.0048\)
\(-0.077\,\%\)		\(0.60\)
✓ OK		\(6.1864\)
\(0.017\,\%\)		\(6.1893\)
\(0.064\,\%\)
\(c_L\)\(0.00940\)\(4 \times 10^{-6}\)\(0.00956\)\(5.8 \times 10^{-5}\)\(+0.00016\)
\(1.7\,\%\)		\(2.51\)
✗ fail		\(0.00951\)
\(1.2\,\%\)		\(0.00973\)
\(3.5\,\%\)
The reference. Braack and Richter give \(c_D = 6.1853\) and \(c_L = 0.00940\) without an uncertainty (printed digits: \(5 \times 10^{-6}\) and \(5 \times 10^{-7}\)). As its uncertainty this report uses the distance to the finest result of an independent high-order code, FeatFlow level 4: \(6.8 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(4 \times 10^{-6}\).
Level by level against the paper's OpenFOAM. Same method family (cell-centred finite volumes, central differences), similar cell counts (Figure 4). Drag error on L1-L4: \(-7.7\,\%\), \(-1.7\,\%\), \(-0.39\,\%\), \(-0.077\,\%\); paper's OpenFOAM: \(-0.83\,\%\), \(0.19\,\%\), \(0.13\,\%\), \(0.064\,\%\). Lift error: \(1.1e+02\,\%\), \(23\,\%\), \(4.4\,\%\), \(1.7\,\%\) against \(84\,\%\), \(17\,\%\), \(6.5\,\%\), \(3.5\,\%\).
The paper's OpenFOAM drag did not converge cleanly. Its changes from level 2 to 3 and 3 to 4 are \(-0.0034\) and \(-0.0043\): they do not shrink, so it cannot be extrapolated; its lift converges with observed order \(1.81\). This simulation converges monotonically in both on L2-L4. FeatFlow (finite elements, more unknowns per cell) is the most accurate of the three on every level.
How stable is the extrapolation? Richardson from L1-L3 gives \(6.1845\) and \(0.00938\); from L2-L4 \(6.1864\) and \(0.00951\). For \(c_D\) the two differ by \(0.0019\), less than the GCI of L4: stable. For \(c_L\) the two differ by \(1.3 \times 10^{-4}\), more than the GCI of L4 (\(5.8 \times 10^{-5}\)): the lift is not yet in its asymptotic range, and its GCI understates the error.
Robustness of the lift (sensitivity runs). Same solver, one change at a time: L3, linear-upwind convection: \(c_D = 6.1715\), \(c_L = 0.00974\) (\(3.6\,\%\)); L3, O-grid radial ratio 2: \(c_D = 6.1638\), \(c_L = 0.00912\) (\(-3\,\%\)); L3, O-grid radial ratio 8: \(c_D = 6.1571\), \(c_L = 0.01032\) (\(9.8\,\%\)); L4, O-grid radial ratio 2: \(c_D = 6.1810\), \(c_L = 0.00938\) (\(-0.27\,\%\)). On L3 the lift spans \(13\,\%\) of the reference between these meshes of the same size while the drag moves by at most \(0.16\,\%\): the lift depends on how the cells are distributed in the O-grid (the flow through the gaps between cylinder and walls), not only on their number. The convection scheme matters little.
A second mesh family. With radial ratio 2 the lift goes from \(0.00912\) (L3) to \(0.00938\) (L4), \(-0.27\,\%\) from the reference, while the production family (ratio 4) gives \(0.00956\). The two families approach the reference from opposite sides; their difference on L4, \(1.8 \times 10^{-4}\), is a more honest measure of the lift's mesh uncertainty than the GCI of one family (\(5.8 \times 10^{-5}\)). The drag of the two families differs by only \(4.8 \times 10^{-4}\).
Pressure and friction. On L4 the pressure gives \(66.7\,\%\) of the drag and friction the rest: at \(Re = 20\) friction is a large part of the drag, unlike at high Reynolds numbers.

8 Workflow insights

Problems met while producing this report, logged at the moment they happened, with how they were solved and what future agents should do differently. These feed back into the workflow guidelines.

gpulogged 2026-11-11 17:27
Problem
environment.md lists the GPU multigrid options to explore as MaxLevels, MinCoarseRows and ZeroGuess. The OGL source (include/OGL/Preconditioner/Multigrid.hpp, CoarseSolver.cpp) reads them in lower camel case (maxLevels, minCoarseRows, smoother, maxIterSmoother, coarseSolver, maxIterCoarse, cycle, reuseHierarchy) and only from a preconditioner SUB-dictionary; there is no ZeroGuess option. Written as top-level keys they would be ignored silently.
Diagnosis
The option names in the guidance were guessed, not read from the plugin. OGL looks the preconditioner options up in the dictionary of the preconditioner entry (preconditioner { preconditioner Multigrid; minCoarseRows 1000; ... }). Its defaults are weak for a large 3D problem: the coarsest level keeps 64000 rows and is 'solved' by ONE Jacobi sweep (coarseSolver Jacobi, maxIterCoarse 1), with one Jacobi smoothing sweep per level.
Fix
Read the option names and defaults from ~/src/OGL before tuning; write them in a preconditioner sub-dictionary (run.py CONFIGS).
Lesson
Read the plugin's source for option names and defaults before tuning; a misspelt option in an OpenFOAM dictionary is ignored without a warning.
Guideline
environment.md, OGL section: replace 'MaxLevels, MinCoarseRows, ZeroGuess' by the real names, show the sub-dictionary form and the defaults (minCoarseRows 64000, coarse solver = 1 Jacobi sweep).

The task brief said to log insights with 'python -m cfdlib.insights add ...'; the CLI verb is 'new' ('add' is rejected by argparse).
Diagnosis
Mismatch between the brief and cfdlib/insights.py.
Fix
Use 'new' (or the Python API insights.log).

Check the CLI help (python -m cfdlib.insights -h) instead of trusting a quoted command.

performancelogged 2026-11-11 17:33
Problem
The study needs the pressure-solve time of CPU runs, but GAMG prints no timings and cfdlib.perf only counts iterations. OpenFOAM's built-in profiling (controlDict: profiling { active true; }) writes /uniform/profiling with the wall time and call count of every section: fvMatrix::solve.p, fvMatrix::solve.U, each function object, for CPU and GPU runs alike (processor0/... in parallel runs).
Diagnosis
Profiling is off by default and not mentioned in the guidelines. One quirk: its GAMG entry 'lduMatrix::solver.coarsestLevelCorr' reports almost the whole pressure solve (a nesting artefact), so only fvMatrix::solve.p is used.
Fix
Profiling on in every run of this case (an output decision); run.py reads the totals per section from processor0.
Lesson
Before writing log parsers for timings, check what the solver can already measure about itself.
Guideline
SKILL.md performance section: switch on controlDict profiling for any performance study and read fvMatrix::solve.; cfdlib.perf.summarize could parse uniform/profiling itself.
gpulogged 2026-11-11 17:33
Problem
OGL's stopping criterion has adaptMinIter (default true): every pressure solve must do at least 0.6 times the iterations of the previous one (log: 'Creating stopping criterion with minIter 421 frequency 6'), and the residual is checked only every few iterations. In a steady SIMPLE run with partial solves (relTol 0.05) this can force far more iterations than the tolerance needs.
Diagnosis
Measured on the 1-million-cell mesh (4 ranks): with OGL's default multigrid, switching adaptMinIter off cut the CG iterations per pressure solve from 132 to 97. With the tuned preconditioner the effect is small (16 with it, 15 without), because the iteration count no longer varies much between solves.
Fix
adaptMinIter false in every tuned GPU configuration (run.py _gpu_mg).
Lesson
Library defaults tuned for transient runs with full solves can waste work in steady runs with partial solves.
Guideline
environment.md OGL section: mention adaptMinIter (default on) and set it off for partial (relTol) solves.
performancelogged 2026-11-11 17:33
Problem
The forces function object costs about 6 % of each iteration on the 2.43 million cell mesh (two calls, cylinder and walls, 0.064 s each per iteration on 16 ranks; profiling): it evaluates the stress tensor on the whole mesh, not only on the patch.
Diagnosis
forces builds devRhoReff (needs grad U everywhere) every call; at 2.4 million cells that is not free.
Fix
Kept every iteration (identical on CPU and GPU runs, so the comparison stays fair) and reported as part of the time outside the pressure solve.
Lesson
Every-iteration function objects are a measurable cost on large meshes and dilute any linear-solver speed-up.
Guideline
For long steady runs, evaluate forces every few iterations (executeInterval) once the stopping rule allows it.
productionlogged 2026-11-11 17:33
Problem
The steady x-momentum balance of the channel closes only to 0.41, 0.28 and 0.23 % of the drag on L1, L2, L3: inside the 0.5 % rule set beforehand, but the imbalance shrinks slowly with refinement, not like a second-order error.
Diagnosis
The balance neglects the viscous normal stress at inlet and outlet. In the continuous problem its integral over the inlet is zero (continuity: the integral of du/dx over a section with no-slip edges vanishes). The discrete one is not: the solver's one-sided face gradient at an inlet whose profile is not the developed duct flow leaves a first-order remainder. Computed from the fields (run.py inletvisc), it is about three quarters of the imbalance on L1-L3; with it, the imbalance falls to about 0.1, 0.07 and 0.055 % of the drag.
Fix
Kept the pass rule fixed beforehand (balance without the term, 0.5 %); report the inlet viscous term and the balance with it as a diagnostic.
Lesson
A conservation check is only as exact as its list of terms: a term that vanishes in the continuum may survive discretely at first order and look like a solver error.
Guideline
primer: for a momentum balance through an inlet with a non-developed profile, include (or measure) the viscous flux through the inlet; it decays only like the first cell size.

monitor.py builds the value with the Unicode sign instead of LaTeX.

analyze.py converts the value to \(\ge 112\) before passing it to the report.

Shared helpers that produce report text must follow the report's typesetting rules too.

cfdlib/monitor.py: write value=m(r'\ge ' + ...) for the projected iteration count.

Problem
The mid-plane picture needs the velocity on the plane z = H/2, which is a face plane of the mesh (even cell count in z). matplotlib's Delaunay triangulation of the structured cell centres has degenerate triangles: plotting works, but LinearTriInterpolator raises 'Triangulation is invalid'. Matching the two cell layers next to the plane by sorted (x, y) also failed until the coordinates were rounded (round-off differences between layers reordered the sort).
Diagnosis
Collinear points of a structured grid; floating-point ties in a lexicographic sort.
Fix
Average the two layers with linear weights after sorting rounded coordinates; interpolate along lines with scipy's LinearNDInterpolator.
Lesson
Structured-grid data and Delaunay-based tools do not mix well; prefer scipy (Qhull) or sampling in OpenFOAM.
Guideline
A helper in cfdlib to extract a plane of a structured mesh (or an OpenFOAM 'surfaces' sampling recipe in the primer) would save every 3D case this detour.
analysislogged 2026-11-11 17:52
Problem
The lift fails the rule fixed beforehand: on L4 it is 1.66 % above the reference, 2.5 times the band (GCI of L4 plus reference uncertainty). Its observed order on L2-L4 is 2.73 (L1-L3: 2.31), so the GCI band is narrow, and the Richardson value is still 1.16 % high. Drag passes (L4 -0.077 %, extrapolated +0.017 %).
Diagnosis
Robustness runs (one change each): convection scheme on L3 moves the lift by 0.8 %; the O-grid radial cell distribution moves it from -3.0 % (ratio 2) through +4.4 % (ratio 4, production) to +9.8 % (ratio 8) of the reference on L3, with the drag almost unchanged. On L4, ratio 2 gives -0.27 % against +1.66 % for ratio 4: the two mesh families approach the reference from opposite sides. The lift, a small difference of large pressure and friction forces, depends on how the gap flow between cylinder and walls is resolved; the GCI of one family (narrow because its observed order is high) does not see that.
Fix
Kept the FAIL verdict of the rule fixed beforehand; reported the sensitivity runs and the spread between the two families as the honest lift uncertainty.
Lesson
For a small force component, one mesh family's GCI can be far too optimistic; a second family (different grading, same cell count) is a cheap and strong test.
Guideline
SKILL.md stage 5: for small or sensitive outputs (lift of a nearly symmetric body), run a second mesh family on at least two levels before trusting the GCI; budget for it in the plan.

Problem
A Python patch of analyze.py passed through a Bash heredoc collapsed every double backslash to a single one. It came out right only because none of the affected sequences formed a control character (TAB from times, form feed from frac); the guideline to edit LaTeX-bearing files only with Edit/Write exists for exactly this.
Diagnosis
The Bash tool processes backslashes before the heredoc reaches Python, whatever the quoting.
Fix
Checked the file for control characters (none) and the edited lines by eye; later edits with the Edit tool.
Lesson
The guideline also applies to small scripted patches, not only to whole files.
Guideline
SKILL.md stage 2: say explicitly that Python one-off patch scripts through Bash count as Bash editing.
performancelogged 2026-11-11 17:58
Problem
OpenFOAM's per-iteration ClockTime in the log, which run.py and case 4 (_loop_us) use for time per iteration, is printed in whole seconds: on a 0.05 s iteration it is useless, on a 0.6 s one it carries a 5-10 % error over 20 iterations. The timeInfo function object's clockTime column has the same 1 s resolution.
Diagnosis
Time::elapsedClockTime returns whole seconds. ExecutionTime (CPU time of rank 0, 0.01 s resolution) looked like wall time on the first checks, but on the 90 thousand cell mesh with 16 ranks it was half the wall time (0.020 against 0.039 s per iteration): with 16 ranks on 16 hardware threads, MPI yields the core instead of busy-waiting. That made 16 ranks look fastest on the small meshes. Profiling's totals (time.run()) are high-resolution wall times.
Fix
Time per iteration = profiled wall time of the iteration loop divided by the iteration count, on both sides (includes the first iteration's one-off costs, the same for every run of a mesh up to the GPU's CUDA start-up).
Lesson
Check the resolution AND the meaning (CPU or wall) of a clock before timing with it, on the smallest case too.
Guideline
cfdlib.perf: compute loop time from ExecutionTime differences (or profiling), never from ClockTime; say in SKILL.md that ClockTime has 1 s resolution.
gpulogged 2026-11-11 18:06
Problem
After the coarse-level fix (CG coarse solve, coarsest level at most 1000 rows) the GPU needed only 15 CG iterations per pressure solve, but the multigrid set-up then cost about 0.9 s per solve on 1 million cells, several times the solve itself, so the GPU was still slower than GAMG.
Diagnosis
OGL rebuilds the multigrid hierarchy (PGM aggregation on the GPU) for every solve by default; a deeper hierarchy costs more to build.
Fix
Reuse the preconditioner for 20 solves (preconditioner { caching 20; }): the pressure matrix changes slowly between SIMPLE iterations, so the stale preconditioner costs about 1-4 extra CG iterations and saves the set-up. reuseHierarchy (recompute only the coarse matrices) helped less.
Lesson
On the GPU, preconditioner set-up can dominate; amortise it over solves.
Guideline
environment.md OGL section: start GPU tuning from minCoarseRows ~1000, coarseSolver CG, maxIterSmoother 2, caching 20, adaptMinIter off (the settings found here), not from the defaults.
performancelogged 2026-11-11 18:39
Problem
The CPU baseline is not 'GAMG on all cores': on this steady 3D case GAMG with the DIC-Gauss-Seidel smoother needs 5 instead of 13 iterations per pressure solve and is about 6 % faster per iteration than with Gauss-Seidel, and 8 ranks beat 16 on every mesh from 0.3 to 4.75 million cells (L4: 1.72 s per iteration on 8 ranks, 1.90 on 16). Case 4 (2D, transient) had found 16 ranks fastest.
Diagnosis
A steady 3D SIMPLE iteration is memory-bandwidth bound; hyper-threads add MPI traffic and halo work without adding bandwidth. DIC smoothing does more per sweep but converges GAMG in fewer cycles.
Fix
The study's CPU baseline is the fastest of GAMG GS / GAMG DIC-GS on 8 or 16 ranks per mesh (4-16 on L4).
Lesson
'Best CPU setup' must be measured for each case; smoother and rank count both matter by 5-15 %.
Guideline
primer, parallel section: add this case's numbers (8 ranks best for steady 3D, DIC-GS smoother) next to case 4's.
gpulogged 2026-11-11 19:15
Problem
Even fully tuned, the GPU only breaks even at about 2 million cells and saves about 11 % of the time per SIMPLE iteration at 4.75 million cells (a factor 1.13), although its pressure solve there is 1.65 times faster than the best GAMG; on a converged L4 run both took about 11.5 minutes.
Diagnosis
Three limits stack up. (1) Amdahl: the pressure solve is only about a third of a steady SIMPLE iteration (momentum, assembly and the force output stay on the CPU), so even an infinitely fast solver gives at most about 1.5 times. (2) Each solve pays a fixed host path: the ranks' matrices are gathered and copied through host memory (no CUDA-aware MPI), tens of milliseconds outside OGL's own timers. (3) The consumer GPU's double precision is slow, so CG with multigrid needs 3 times the iterations of GAMG with DIC smoothing and gains only from memory bandwidth.
Fix
Reported as the answer: break-even and gains measured, with the same converged forces on both sides.
Lesson
For steady incompressible OpenFOAM runs, offloading only the pressure solve cannot give more than the pressure share allows; measure that share first (profiling) before investing in GPU tuning.
Guideline
SKILL.md performance study: start by measuring the pressure share with profiling and state the Amdahl bound; it sets expectations before any GPU run.
